title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the k-th largest element in the array. This is the k-th largest in sorted order, not the k-th distinct element.
realWorld: Service-level objectives are this problem: the p99 latency of a request is the k-th largest response time for k = 1% of the sample. Monitoring systems compute it continuously over a window of millions of measurements, which is why they never sort.

examples.explanation: Sorted descending: [6,5,5,4,3,3,2,2,1]. The 4th is 4. Duplicates count separately — 5 appears twice and occupies two positions.
The largest element of a one-element array.

constraints: k is always valid — there are at least k elements

bruteForce.idea: Sort the array descending and index into position k-1.
code: public static int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
Arrays.sort(nums);                  // ascending, O(n log n)
return nums[nums.length - k];       // …and we read exactly one of them

complexity.space: O(log n) for the sort's recursion, or O(n) if you box the values to sort descending

bruteForce.whySlow: The question asks for one element. Sorting determines the exact rank of all n, including the full internal ordering of the n-k elements that lose and the k-1 that beat the answer — none of which is read. For n = 100,000 that is roughly 1.7 million comparisons to produce a single number. It also mutates the caller's array, which is a real side effect if the array is reused.

patternIdentification: 'The k-th largest' is a top-k question in disguise: the k-th largest is the *smallest* of the k largest. So if you can maintain the k largest elements seen so far, the answer is whichever of them is weakest — and a min-heap of size k puts exactly that element at its root, in O(1). The signal is that k is bounded and small while n is large, and that no element outside the top k ever matters.

optimized.idea: Sweep the array once, keeping a min-heap capped at k. While the heap is short of k, everything goes in. After that, a value only matters if it beats the heap's root — the weakest element currently being kept. If it does, evict the root and insert the value; if it does not, it can never be in the top k and is dropped with a single comparison. At the end the heap holds the k largest and its root is the k-th largest.
code: import java.util.PriorityQueue;
/** O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Does not mutate nums. */
public static int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
PriorityQueue<Integer> keep = new PriorityQueue<>();   // MIN-heap of the k largest so far
for (int value : nums) {
if (keep.size() < k) {
keep.offer(value);
} else if (value > keep.peek()) {   // beats the weakest survivor?
keep.poll();                    // evict the weakest
keep.offer(value);
// else: it cannot displace anyone — one comparison, no heap work
return keep.peek();   // the weakest of the k largest IS the k-th largest

visualization.title: k = 3: the heap only ever holds three values, and its root is the answer
code: PriorityQueue<Integer> keep = new PriorityQueue<>();   // MIN-heap of the k largest so far
for (int value : nums) {
if (keep.size() < k) keep.offer(value);            // not full yet — everything qualifies
else if (value > keep.peek()) {                    // beats the weakest survivor?
keep.poll(); keep.offer(value);                // evict the weakest, keep this one
// else: value <= keep.peek(), so it can never be top-k — drop it
return keep.peek();                                    // the k-th largest

commonMistakes: Using a max-heap of size k. The root would then be the *largest* of the ones you kept, which you never need; you need the weakest, because that is the only element eviction can ever target. Use a min-heap.
Offering every element and then polling k times. That is a heap of size n — O(n log n) time and O(n) space, i.e. the brute force with extra machinery. The cap at k is the entire optimisation.
Returning `keep.poll()` instead of `keep.peek()` when the caller may reuse the heap, or confusing the two while debugging. Both return the root; `poll` also removes it.
Treating duplicates as one element. With nums = [3,3,3] and k = 2 the answer is 3; the problem ranks positions, not distinct values. Do not de-duplicate.
Off-by-one between 'k-th largest' and 'index k' — after an ascending sort the k-th largest is at `nums.length - k`, not at `k` or `k - 1`.
Unboxing `keep.peek()` without checking for an empty heap. If k is 0 or the array is empty, `peek()` returns null and the implicit `intValue()` throws a NullPointerException far from the real cause.
